title: Distributed single-source shortest paths
summary: Use network latency as edge weight and compare synchronous versus asynchronous Bellman–Ford in a message-passing system.
objectives: Explain the termination and message-complexity trade-off

sourceLens.whyExaminable: The lecture contrasts a round-based synchronous relaxation with an event-driven asynchronous relaxation; the algorithm and termination boundary are the examinable distinction.

sections.title: The objective
sections.body: The sender is the source node. Each process must learn the shortest path from that sender, where an edge weight represents network latency. A broadcast tree is therefore an optimization problem: find a low-latency path to every process.

sections.title: Relaxation and rounds
sections.body: In synchronous Bellman–Ford, each round propagates the best known distance through neighbors. After $n-1$ rounds, shortest paths are found under the lecture's assumptions. The asynchronous version sends an update when a process improves its local estimate and has no fixed round count.

math.name: Bellman–Ford relaxation
math.purpose: Update the shortest known distance to process $p_i$ from neighbor estimates.
math.explanation: The candidate path through neighbor $p_j$ has length $\ell_j+w_{j,i}$; keep the smallest candidate.

examples.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous
steps: Synchronous: all processes advance together by rounds.
Asynchronous: an improved estimate triggers a message.
Synchronous termination is fixed at $n-1$ rounds.
Asynchronous termination requires detecting that no further update is in flight.
examples.answer: Synchronous execution is easier to reason about but waits at round boundaries; asynchronous execution can exploit early improvements but needs a termination condition.

contrastDrills.prompt: Which version has a fixed $n-1$ round bound in the lecture?
contrastDrills.explanation: The synchronous algorithm terminates after $n-1$ rounds; the asynchronous version has no fixed round termination condition.
contrastDrills.misconception: Message-triggered progress is not the same as a global round.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is a shortest-path broadcast more than simply sending the message to everyone?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate reachability from the latency of the path used to reach each process.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Broadcast guarantees reach all processes, but the shortest-path problem asks every process to learn the minimum-latency route from the source. The communication tree must therefore be optimized.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why does asynchronous Bellman–Ford need a different termination argument from the synchronous version?
criticalQuestions.angle: Separate a fixed round bound from the possibility of delayed messages or updates still in flight.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: Synchronous Bellman–Ford has a global round structure and terminates after the stated $n-1$ rounds. Asynchronous Bellman–Ford is event-driven, so it must establish that no improving update remains in flight and no process can improve its estimate.
